questions.stem: This Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear shows a distinctive crescent (banana) shaped intracellular form. This morphology is characteristic of which organism?

explanation.summary: Unlike the round gametocytes of other Plasmodium species, P. falciparum produces a characteristic elongated crescent- or banana-shaped gametocyte, which is diagnostically distinctive on a blood smear.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike the round gametocytes of other Plasmodium species, P. falciparum produces a characteristic elongated crescent- or banana-shaped gametocyte, which is diagnostically distinctive on a blood smear.

questions.stem: These three peripheral blood smear fields show dark-stained inclusions located within red blood cells. These findings are most consistent with infection by which class of organism?

explanation.summary: The dark-stained organisms lie inside the erythrocytes, a hallmark of intraerythrocytic malarial parasites. Bacteria, viral inclusions, and yeast forms would not produce this intra-RBC parasitized appearance across multiple fields.
explanation.whyCorrect: The dark-stained organisms lie inside the erythrocytes, a hallmark of intraerythrocytic malarial parasites. Bacteria, viral inclusions, and yeast forms would not produce this intra-RBC parasitized appearance across multiple fields.

questions.stem: This blood smear shows organisms within red blood cells arranged as a four-part tetrad (compared with the cross shown for reference). This finding is characteristic of which infection?

explanation.summary: Babesia merozoites form a tetrad within the RBC that resembles a Maltese cross, a finding specific to babesiosis. Plasmodium does not form tetrads, and Trypanosoma and Bartonella have different smear appearances.
explanation.whyCorrect: Babesia merozoites form a tetrad within the RBC that resembles a Maltese cross, a finding specific to babesiosis. Plasmodium does not form tetrads, and Trypanosoma and Bartonella have different smear appearances.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Plasmodium, Babesia, and Brucella
questions.stem: The adverse reactions illustrated are caused by an antimalarial drug. By what mechanism does this drug kill the parasite?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibits mitochondrial electron transport of the parasite

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: D
choices.text: Binds parasite DNA and disrupts mitochondrial function

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibits conversion of toxic heme to hemozoin

explanation.summary: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine block detoxification of heme to hemozoin and increase digestive-vacuole pH, causing accumulation of toxic heme that damages the parasite. Their adverse effects include pruritus, cardiomyopathy, and hemolysis (especially in G6PD deficiency).
explanation.whyCorrect: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine block detoxification of heme to hemozoin and increase digestive-vacuole pH, causing accumulation of toxic heme that damages the parasite. Their adverse effects include pruritus, cardiomyopathy, and hemolysis (especially in G6PD deficiency).

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Plasmodium, Babesia, and Brucella
questions.stem: The adverse reactions shown belong to a first-line combination prophylaxis. What is the combined mechanism of its two components?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds parasite DNA and disrupts mitochondria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits mitochondrial electron transport and blocks folate synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits heme detoxification within the digestive vacuole

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit

explanation.summary: Atovaquone selectively inhibits parasite mitochondrial electron transport, while proguanil's metabolite inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking folate/DNA synthesis. Common adverse effects include nausea, abdominal pain, and transaminitis (increased AST/ALT).
explanation.whyCorrect: Atovaquone selectively inhibits parasite mitochondrial electron transport, while proguanil's metabolite inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking folate/DNA synthesis. Common adverse effects include nausea, abdominal pain, and transaminitis (increased AST/ALT).

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Plasmodium, Babesia, and Brucella
questions.stem: The adverse effects depicted are associated with a tetracycline-class antimalarial. What is its mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binds parasite DNA and disrupts mitochondria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits heme detoxification in the digestive vacuole

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cleaves an endoperoxide bridge to generate free radicals

explanation.summary: Doxycycline is a 30S protein-synthesis inhibitor that prevents the parasite from replicating. Its adverse effects include GI disturbances (diarrhea, vomiting, nausea) and photosensitivity, plus chelation with cations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Doxycycline is a 30S protein-synthesis inhibitor that prevents the parasite from replicating. Its adverse effects include GI disturbances (diarrhea, vomiting, nausea) and photosensitivity, plus chelation with cations.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Plasmodium, Babesia, and Brucella
questions.stem: The adverse effects shown are caused by an antimalarial used to prevent relapse of P. ovale and P. vivax. What is its mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibits heme detoxification in the digestive vacuole

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interferes with 80S protein synthesis and heme digestion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disrupts parasite mitochondrial function and binds parasite DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits mitochondrial electron transport and folate synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit

explanation.summary: Primaquine disrupts mitochondria and binds parasite DNA, and is uniquely active against exoerythrocytic (hypnozoite) stages. Its adverse effects include cardiac arrhythmias (QT prolongation), leukopenia, and hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primaquine disrupts mitochondria and binds parasite DNA, and is uniquely active against exoerythrocytic (hypnozoite) stages. Its adverse effects include cardiac arrhythmias (QT prolongation), leukopenia, and hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: This colorized transmission electron micrograph shows virions of a hemorrhagic fever virus family. Which structural feature is characteristic of the particles shown?

explanation.summary: The image shows long, thread-like enveloped virions typical of the Filoviridae family (Marburg/Ebola), which have a helical nucleocapsid enclosed in an envelope and a filamentous morphology.
explanation.whyCorrect: The image shows long, thread-like enveloped virions typical of the Filoviridae family (Marburg/Ebola), which have a helical nucleocapsid enclosed in an envelope and a filamentous morphology.

questions.stem: This animal appears in a section on filovirus transmission. What is its epidemiologic role for Marburg virus?

explanation.summary: Bats serve as the natural reservoir for Marburg virus and the likely reservoir for Ebola virus; spillover into humans occurs through contact with infected animal fluids.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bats serve as the natural reservoir for Marburg virus and the likely reservoir for Ebola virus; spillover into humans occurs through contact with infected animal fluids.

questions.stem: This animal is shown in the hantavirus epidemiology section. How do humans most commonly acquire hantavirus infection from it?

explanation.summary: Rodents are the reservoir for hantaviruses; humans are infected mainly by inhaling aerosolized particles from rodent feces, urine, and saliva.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rodents are the reservoir for hantaviruses; humans are infected mainly by inhaling aerosolized particles from rodent feces, urine, and saliva.

questions.stem: This schematic maps where FDA-approved monoclonal antibody therapies bind on the Ebola virus surface glycoprotein. By what mechanism do these antibodies neutralize the virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking glycoprotein binding to host cell receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking viral budding from the membrane

explanation.summary: The monoclonal antibodies bind the viral surface glycoprotein and block its engagement of cognate host receptors, neutralizing the virus; they also mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The monoclonal antibodies bind the viral surface glycoprotein and block its engagement of cognate host receptors, neutralizing the virus; they also mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.

questions.stem: In this liver histology from a fatal yellow fever case, the arrows indicate small, shrunken, intensely eosinophilic hepatocytes that lack or have a pyknotic nucleus. What cellular process do these bodies represent?

explanation.summary: The arrowed structures are Councilman (acidophil) bodies, hepatocytes dying by apoptosis. They shrink, become deeply eosinophilic, and lose their nucleus, distinguishing them from swollen or fat-laden cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The arrowed structures are Councilman (acidophil) bodies, hepatocytes dying by apoptosis. They shrink, become deeply eosinophilic, and lose their nucleus, distinguishing them from swollen or fat-laden cells.

questions.stem: In this classification chart of viral hemorrhagic fever agents, what single feature separates the viruses placed in the green 'Arboviruses' branch from those in the blue 'Not Arboviruses' branch?

explanation.summary: Arbovirus means arthropod-borne virus. The green branch (yellow fever, dengue, Zika, West Nile, chikungunya, Rift Valley, CCHF) is spread by mosquitoes or ticks, whereas the blue branch (Ebola, Marburg, hantavirus, Lassa) is acquired from bat or rodent contact, not a vector.
explanation.whyCorrect: Arbovirus means arthropod-borne virus. The green branch (yellow fever, dengue, Zika, West Nile, chikungunya, Rift Valley, CCHF) is spread by mosquitoes or ticks, whereas the blue branch (Ebola, Marburg, hantavirus, Lassa) is acquired from bat or rodent contact, not a vector.

questions.stem: This historical series of portraits illustrates a clinical course progressing from fever and flushing to marked scleral/skin yellowing and finally to hemorrhage with black (coffee-ground) vomit. Which disease is being depicted?

explanation.summary: The sequence shows the classic toxic phase of yellow fever: high fever followed by jaundice (hence the name) from hepatic injury, then mucosal erosion and hematemesis of partially digested blood ('black vomit').
explanation.whyCorrect: The sequence shows the classic toxic phase of yellow fever: high fever followed by jaundice (hence the name) from hepatic injury, then mucosal erosion and hematemesis of partially digested blood ('black vomit').

questions.stem: These images of an infant show cranial/skull irregularities, redundant scalp folds, and a lateral skull radiograph demonstrating a strikingly small calvarium. Congenital infection by which virus is responsible for this pattern?

explanation.summary: Congenital Zika syndrome results from vertical (transplacental) transmission and characteristically produces microcephaly with overlapping skull sutures, redundant scalp skin, ventriculomegaly, and intracranial calcifications.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congenital Zika syndrome results from vertical (transplacental) transmission and characteristically produces microcephaly with overlapping skull sutures, redundant scalp skin, ventriculomegaly, and intracranial calcifications.
